questions.stem: A strategy profile is a Nash equilibrium when…
options: No player can gain by changing their own strategy alone
Every player gets the highest payoff in the game
Players together cannot do any better
Every player plays a dominant strategy
questions.explanation: In a Nash equilibrium every strategy is a best response to the others, so no one gains from a unilateral change (Slide 3). It need not be the best joint outcome (Slide 4).
questions.hint: Think about one player deviating on their own.

questions.stem: In the Prisoner's Dilemma, (Defect, Defect) is…
options: A Nash equilibrium that is not Pareto optimal
Pareto optimal but not a Nash equilibrium
Both a Nash equilibrium and Pareto optimal
Neither a Nash equilibrium nor Pareto optimal
questions.explanation: Neither player gains by switching alone, so it is a Nash equilibrium, but both would prefer (Cooperate, Cooperate), so it is not Pareto optimal (Slide 4).
questions.hint: Check unilateral deviation, then check whether both could do better together.

questions.leadIn: When there is more than one (Slide 5).
questions.stem: Driving on the left or the right is an example of…
options: A coordination game with two Nash equilibria
A game with no Nash equilibrium
A game where one strategy strictly dominates
questions.explanation: Both (left, left) and (right, right) are equilibria; conventions decide which one is played (Slide 5).
questions.hint: Both conventions work as long as everyone agrees.
